_notes: Edit this file, not the code, when the client changes content scope, concept lists, Bloom targets, misconceptions, checkpoint items, or the comparative-evaluation pairing. Pairing matches HLD Section 6.4 and the D-03 decision-log entry: Bloom-tier matching within a module. D-03 stays OPEN until a TA/instructor has done the 'equally hard to a first-year' check on each pair -- flip difficulty_reviewed per pair once that happens (see app.content.loader.mark_pair_reviewed / POST /topics/pairs/{pair_id}/mark-reviewed). Two concepts are Understand/Analyse-only within their module and are intentionally excluded from graded_pairs -> they go in general_use_only.

misconceptions.statement: Draws the boundary loosely, so energy leaving the system is counted as if it had vanished rather than entering the surroundings
misconceptions.probe: Before any numbers: point at exactly what is inside your system. The energy that left it — where is it now?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Deciding what counts as 'the system' before doing the accounting

misconceptions.statement: Talks about the heat 'contained in' a system, treating heat as a stored property rather than energy in transit across a boundary
misconceptions.probe: Can you tell me how much heat is in this gas right now? If not, what quantity were you reaching for?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Heat is a transfer, not something a system holds

misconceptions.statement: Assumes Q and W are fixed by the endpoints because delta-U is, so any path between two states is treated as interchangeable
misconceptions.probe: Two different paths take this gas between the same two states. Which of delta-U, Q and W must come out the same, and which need not?
misconceptions.learner_facing: delta-U depends only on the endpoints; Q and W depend on the route

blanks.prompt: Of the three quantities in delta-U = Q - W, the one fixed entirely by the initial and final states is ____.
blanks.hint: Two of the three depend on how you got there. One does not.

blanks.prompt: Energy that leaves the system as heat does not disappear — it is now in the ____.
blanks.hint: The accounting has exactly two columns.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A gas is compressed, and during the compression it also gives off heat. Account for the energy: say what happens to the internal energy and why, naming where each quantity goes.
rubric: Identifies work done ON the gas as energy entering the system
Identifies heat given off as energy leaving the system to the surroundings
Concludes delta-U is the net of the two, rather than guessing a direction
Keeps the system boundary explicit throughout

checkpoint_items.prompt: Two processes take the same gas from state A to state B by different routes. A classmate says 'same endpoints, so Q must be the same both times.' Is that right? Explain.
rubric: Says no
States that delta-U is the same because internal energy is a state function
States that Q and W individually depend on the path
Notes that Q - W is nonetheless the same for both routes

concepts.name: Sign conventions for work and heat

misconceptions.statement: Applies the formula without first fixing which direction counts as positive, so work done by and work done on the system get the same sign
misconceptions.probe: Work is done BY the gas as it expands. In the convention you are using, is W positive or negative?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Stating which direction is positive before substituting numbers

misconceptions.statement: Starts in delta-U = Q - W and finishes in delta-U = Q + W, switching convention partway so the answer flips sign
misconceptions.probe: Read back the form of the first law you wrote down, then the one you used at the end. Are they the same statement?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Staying in one convention from start to finish

misconceptions.statement: Treats a negative Q or W as an error or an impossibility rather than as a direction of transfer
misconceptions.probe: Your answer came out as W = -200 J. What physical situation does that minus sign describe?
misconceptions.learner_facing: A minus sign is a direction, not a mistake

blanks.prompt: Using the convention delta-U = Q - W, where W is work done BY the gas: during an expansion, W is ____.
expected_answers: positive because the gas does work
blanks.hint: The gas is the one doing the pushing here.

blanks.prompt: A system releases heat to its surroundings. In the standard convention, Q is ____.
expected_answers: negative because heat leaves the system
blanks.hint: Energy is leaving the thing you are accounting for.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and expands, doing 200 J of work on its surroundings. State your sign convention, then find delta-U.
rubric: States the convention explicitly before substituting
Assigns Q = +500 J (heat into the system)
Assigns W consistently with the stated convention
Arrives at delta-U = +300 J
Uses one convention throughout without switching

checkpoint_items.prompt: A classmate computes W = -350 J for a process and says the answer must be wrong because work cannot be negative. What would you tell them?
rubric: Says the negative value is not an error
Explains that the sign encodes direction of transfer
Names which direction the minus sign corresponds to under a stated convention

misconceptions.statement: Reads reversible as 'can be run backwards', so any process with a physical return path is called reversible
misconceptions.probe: You can certainly push that piston back to where it started. What else has to be true for the process to count as reversible?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Reversible means system AND surroundings both return, leaving no trace

misconceptions.statement: Treats slowness as sufficient: assumes any quasi-static process is reversible, overlooking dissipation
misconceptions.probe: This compression is infinitely slow, but the piston rubs against the cylinder wall. Reversible?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Slow is necessary but not enough — dissipation still spoils it

misconceptions.statement: Attributes irreversibility entirely to how fast the process runs, missing friction, mixing and finite temperature differences as sources
misconceptions.probe: Can you name a process that stays irreversible no matter how slowly you run it?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Irreversibility has several sources, not just speed

blanks.prompt: A process counts as reversible only if both the system and the ____ can be returned to their initial states with no net change.
blanks.hint: Returning the system alone is the easy half.

blanks.prompt: An infinitely slow compression with friction at the piston wall is still irreversible, because friction causes ____.
blanks.hint: Something is generated that you cannot un-generate.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A gas is compressed infinitely slowly, but there is friction between the piston and the cylinder. A classmate calls this reversible because it is quasi-static. Analyse their claim.
rubric: Says the process is not reversible
Accepts that quasi-static is necessary but argues it is not sufficient
Identifies friction as dissipation / entropy generation
Connects to the requirement that the surroundings also return unchanged

checkpoint_items.prompt: Give one process that can be physically run backwards but is still irreversible, and say what makes it so.
rubric: Gives a concrete process with a physical return path
Identifies a source of irreversibility (friction, mixing, finite temperature difference, free expansion)
Explains that restoring the system leaves a net change in the surroundings

concepts.name: Entropy of the universe in a spontaneous process

misconceptions.statement: Requires the system's own entropy to increase in any spontaneous process, so exothermic ordering processes like freezing look like violations
misconceptions.probe: Water freezing below 0 C is spontaneous, and the ice is more ordered than the liquid. Which entropy is it that has to increase?
misconceptions.learner_facing: It is the total entropy that must increase, not the system's

misconceptions.statement: Computes delta-S for the system and stops, never evaluating the surroundings' contribution to the total
misconceptions.probe: You have delta-S_system. What is the other term you need before you can call this spontaneous?
misconceptions.learner_facing: The surroundings' entropy change is half the calculation

misconceptions.statement: Reasons about entropy purely as visual messiness, so it cannot be compared or computed for processes where 'tidiness' is ambiguous
misconceptions.probe: Two gases mix at constant temperature — can you quantify the entropy change, rather than judging whether it looks messier?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Entropy is a measurable quantity, not just 'disorder'

blanks.prompt: For any spontaneous process, the quantity that must increase is the entropy of the ____.
blanks.hint: Not the system on its own.

blanks.prompt: When water freezes spontaneously below 0 C, the system's entropy decreases, so the entropy of the ____ must increase by more.
blanks.hint: Where did the released heat go?

checkpoint_items.prompt: Water freezing at -10 C is spontaneous, yet ice is more ordered than liquid water. Explain why this does not violate the second law.
rubric: Identifies that the system's entropy does decrease
Identifies heat released to the surroundings
States that the surroundings' entropy increase exceeds the system's decrease
Concludes the total entropy change is positive

checkpoint_items.prompt: A classmate judges spontaneity by computing delta-S for the system only. Describe a case where this gives them the wrong answer, and say what they left out.
rubric: Gives a case with negative delta-S_system that is nonetheless spontaneous
Names the missing term as the surroundings' entropy change
States the correct criterion in terms of total entropy

misconceptions.statement: Holds entropy and visual disorder to be the same thing, so a tidy room or a crystal is read as low entropy on sight
misconceptions.probe: A tidy drawer and a messy one at the same temperature — can you actually rank their entropies by looking?
misconceptions.learner_facing: 'Disorder' is an analogy; entropy is a defined quantity

misconceptions.statement: Reads the second law as forbidding any entropy decrease anywhere, so refrigerators and living things look like violations
misconceptions.probe: Your fridge lowers the entropy of the food inside it. Which system does the second law actually constrain?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Local decreases are fine; the total is what cannot decrease

blanks.prompt: The second law says entropy cannot decrease in a(n) ____ system.
blanks.hint: The constraint is on a system exchanging nothing with anything.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A refrigerator makes the air inside it colder and more ordered. Explain, in your own words, why this is not a violation of the second law.
rubric: Accepts that entropy inside the fridge decreases
Identifies that the fridge exhausts heat to the room
States that the total entropy of fridge plus room increases
Distinguishes a local decrease from a total decrease

misconceptions.statement: Reads P(A given B) as though it meant P(B given A), treating the two as interchangeable
misconceptions.probe: P(cough given flu) is high — does that make P(flu given cough) high too, and why?
misconceptions.learner_facing: P(A given B) and P(B given A) are different questions

misconceptions.statement: Uses P(A and B) where P(A given B) is asked, skipping the division by P(B)
misconceptions.probe: You want the probability among the B cases only. What do you have to divide by to restrict attention to those?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Conditioning shrinks the sample space — that is the division step

misconceptions.statement: Keeps computing over the full sample space after conditioning, rather than over the subset where the condition holds
misconceptions.probe: Once you are told B happened, which outcomes are still in play?
misconceptions.learner_facing: After 'given B', only the B outcomes count

blanks.prompt: By definition, P(A given B) equals P(A and B) divided by ____.
blanks.hint: You are restricting attention to the cases where the condition holds.

blanks.prompt: Conditioning on B means the sample space is reduced to only the outcomes in which B ____.
blanks.hint: Everything outside B is off the table now.

checkpoint_items.prompt: Nearly everyone with flu has a cough, so P(cough given flu) is about 0.9. Does it follow that P(flu given cough) is about 0.9? Explain.
rubric: Says no
Explains that the two conditionals have different conditioning events
Refers to how common coughs are overall (or how common flu is) as the reason they differ
Does not simply assert the numbers are equal

checkpoint_items.prompt: In your own words, say what changes about the sample space when you are told that B has happened, and why that introduces a division.
rubric: States that the sample space is restricted to outcomes where B holds
Identifies P(B) as the size of that restricted space
Connects the division to renormalising within the restricted space

misconceptions.statement: Uses independent and mutually exclusive as synonyms, so 'cannot happen together' and 'do not affect each other' get the same test
misconceptions.probe: Two events cannot both happen. Does knowing A happened tell you anything about B?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Independent and mutually exclusive are different, almost opposite, ideas

misconceptions.statement: Infers independence from disjointness, missing that two mutually exclusive events with nonzero probability are necessarily dependent
misconceptions.probe: If A and B are disjoint and A happened, what is P(B) now? Is that the same as P(B) before?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Disjoint events are dependent: one happening rules the other out

misconceptions.statement: Adds probabilities to get P(A and B) or multiplies to get P(A or B), picking the rule by habit rather than by which property holds
misconceptions.probe: Which property did you check before choosing to multiply — independence, or disjointness?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Multiply for 'and' under independence; add for 'or' under disjointness

blanks.prompt: If A and B are mutually exclusive, then P(A and B) = ____.
A and B are independent exactly when P(A and B) equals P(A) times ____.
blanks.hint: This is the definition, not a consequence.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A single die roll gives a 2, or gives a 5 — call these A and B. Are A and B mutually exclusive? Are they independent? Justify each answer separately.
rubric: Says A and B are mutually exclusive
Says A and B are NOT independent
Justifies dependence via P(A and B) = 0 not equalling P(A)P(B)
Treats the two properties as separate tests rather than one

checkpoint_items.prompt: Give one pair of events that is independent but not mutually exclusive, and say which test you applied.
rubric: Gives a valid example (e.g. two separate coin flips, or rain today and a coin flip)
Shows P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) or argues one does not inform the other
Notes the events can occur together, so they are not disjoint

misconceptions.statement: Reasons from the test's accuracy alone, leaving the prevalence of the condition out of the calculation entirely
misconceptions.probe: The test is 99% accurate. Before we go further — out of 10,000 people, how many actually have the condition?
misconceptions.learner_facing: How rare the condition is changes the answer as much as the test quality

misconceptions.statement: Reports P(positive given disease) as the answer when P(disease given positive) was asked
misconceptions.probe: Which of those two probabilities does the patient in front of you actually want to know?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Test accuracy and 'do I have it' are different conditionals

misconceptions.statement: Compares true positives against the whole population rather than against all positives, so the false positives from a large healthy group are omitted from the denominator
misconceptions.probe: Your denominator should be everyone who tested positive. Did you include the healthy people who tested positive too?
misconceptions.learner_facing: A rare condition means most positives come from the healthy majority

blanks.prompt: To get P(disease given positive), the denominator must be the total number of ____ results.
blanks.hint: Both the sick and the healthy contribute to it.

blanks.prompt: In Bayes' theorem, the probability of the condition before any test result is called the ____.
blanks.hint: It is the piece people leave out.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test catches 99% of real cases and has a 5% false positive rate. Someone tests positive. Work out roughly how likely it is that they have the disease, showing your reasoning.
rubric: Uses the 1 in 1000 base rate in the calculation
Counts true positives from the diseased group
Counts false positives from the healthy group
Divides true positives by ALL positives
Arrives at a low posterior (roughly 2%) and is not surprised into discarding it

checkpoint_items.prompt: A classmate answers '99%' to the question above because the test is 99% accurate. Name the error they made and which quantity they actually computed.
rubric: Identifies the error as base rate neglect or as flipping the conditional
States that 99% is P(positive given disease), i.e. sensitivity
States that the question asked for P(disease given positive)

misconceptions.statement: Uses the standard error and the population standard deviation interchangeably, so sample size never enters the answer
misconceptions.probe: You quadrupled the sample size. Which of the two numbers changed, and by how much?
misconceptions.learner_facing: SD describes individuals; SE describes the sample mean

misconceptions.statement: Interprets the standard error as the spread of individual observations rather than the spread of the sample mean across repeated samples
misconceptions.probe: SE = 2. Is that telling you how much one person varies, or how much the average of your sample would jump if you drew it again?
misconceptions.learner_facing: SE is about how much your average would move, not how people differ

misconceptions.statement: Expects the standard error to halve when the sample size doubles, applying linear rather than root-n scaling
misconceptions.probe: To halve the standard error, by what factor do you have to multiply n?
misconceptions.learner_facing: SE shrinks with the square root of n, not with n

blanks.prompt: The standard error of the mean equals the standard deviation divided by the square root of ____.
blanks.hint: The only quantity here that you control.

blanks.prompt: To halve the standard error, you must multiply the sample size by ____.
blanks.hint: The square root is doing the work.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A population has SD = 10. You take samples of size 25. Find the standard error, then say what would happen to it if you took samples of size 100 instead, and why.
rubric: Computes SE = 2 for n = 25
Computes SE = 1 for n = 100
Attributes the change to division by the square root of n
Notes the population SD itself is unchanged by sampling more

checkpoint_items.prompt: Your sample of 40 students has a mean study time of 12 hours with SE = 0.5. A classmate concludes that most students study between 11.5 and 12.5 hours. What have they misread?
rubric: Identifies that SE describes the sampling distribution of the mean
States that individual spread is given by the SD, not the SE
Notes the interval describes uncertainty in the mean, not the range of students

concepts.name: Correlation and causation in a fitted model

misconceptions.statement: Reads a fitted regression coefficient from observational data as the causal effect of intervening on that predictor
misconceptions.probe: Your model says 2.3 per unit. If we went out and raised that predictor by one unit ourselves, would we get 2.3?
misconceptions.learner_facing: A fitted slope is an association until the design earns a causal reading

misconceptions.statement: Treats a high R-squared as evidence that the predictors cause the outcome, conflating fit quality with causal validity
misconceptions.probe: A model with R-squared of 0.95 predicts ice cream sales from drowning rates. Is the causal story settled?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Good fit and correct causal story are separate claims

misconceptions.statement: Concludes causation from an association without proposing any third variable that could produce it
misconceptions.probe: Name one variable that could drive both of these at once. What happens to your claim if it exists?
misconceptions.learner_facing: Always name a candidate confounder before claiming cause

blanks.prompt: A third variable that influences both the predictor and the outcome, creating an association with no direct causal link, is called a ____.
blanks.hint: It is the variable you did not put in the model.

blanks.prompt: The design that most directly licenses a causal reading of a coefficient is a randomised ____.
blanks.hint: Randomisation is what breaks the link to confounders.

checkpoint_items.prompt: A model fitted to observational data finds that students who attend more tutorials score 8 marks higher, with R-squared of 0.6. A classmate concludes tutorials raise marks by 8. Analyse this claim.
rubric: Identifies the coefficient as an association, not an intervention effect
Proposes at least one concrete confounder (e.g. prior motivation or ability)
States that R-squared speaks to fit, not to causal validity
Names what design or adjustment would be needed to support the causal claim

checkpoint_items.prompt: Explain what would have to change about how the tutorial data was collected before the 8-mark figure could be read as a causal effect.
rubric: Proposes randomised assignment to tutorials, or a credible quasi-experimental design
Explains that randomisation breaks the association between the predictor and confounders
Acknowledges remaining limits (compliance, external validity) or the need to adjust for measured confounders

basic_student.role: forces the definition into other words; asks questions a self-conscious learner would suppress

advanced_student.role: introduces a worked situation, then probes boundaries and edge cases

_content_notes: Each concept carries the authored half of the structured record (PROJECT.md D5 / HLD T1.7): key_terms, misconceptions, blanks and checkpoint_items with rubrics. The compiled half (claims, worked_example, hint_ladder) is produced by services/verification_engine at build time and is NOT stored here. misconception ids are an enum: every misconception_id and targets_misconception value must name a misconception declared on the same concept, and DoubtLogEntry.misconception_id draws from this list -- that is what makes doubts countable rather than a pile of strings. content_reviewed is false until a TA/instructor has checked the misconceptions and rubrics for a concept; POST /topics/concepts/{concept_id}/mark-content-reviewed flips it, and /topics/content-review-status reports which are outstanding. blanks carry expected_answers, which are server-side only and are never sent to the browser.
